In a flat of three, nobody holds authority over anybody; any chore arrangement one member designs, records and runs is experienced by the other two as being managed. On that reading, the two headline symptoms stop looking like separate defects. Reinterpreting an agreement later is what enforcement looks like when there is no authority to enforce with; withdrawing from the talks is what objection looks like when there is no comfortable way to voice it. If that framing is even partly right, the goal is not clarity alone but legitimacy — and legitimacy is made by who owns the design, not by how well the design is written.

First move: assign spaces, not shares. Most 'what did we agree' disputes attach to the seams between two people's contributions — I did the counters, you said you'd do the floor, whose job was the hob? Give each common area a single owner, answerable end to end, and the seams vanish; inside someone's domain there is nothing left for two honest memories to disagree about. To allocate without a live negotiation the avoidant friend can simply not attend, collect private, asynchronous rankings — message everyone the list of areas and ask which they mind most and least — and match owners to tolerances. Set one written floor for common areas at a level all three can genuinely accept, not at the cleanest person's preference: a floor set at the highest standard just reproduces the imposition. Within a domain the owner may exceed the floor as they please; below it, they answer to the text.

Second move: put the specification where the work happens, not where the talk happens. A checklist inside the cupboard door, taped to the bin lid, on the bathroom mirror — counters cleared and wiped, floor swept, bin out — beats a confirmation posted after a conversation, because the artifact does not depend on anyone convening anything. It survives schedule chaos, it can be consulted by whoever is actually doing the task at the moment they do it, and it gives the friend who avoids conversations a way to know and meet the standard without having one. Add a single gap-filler rule agreed once: where nothing is written at the spot, the default is X. After that, memory has nothing to be about.

Third move: rotate the chair. Whoever convenes, records and adjusts the arrangements holds a kind of office; if that is always the asker, then 'the system' and 'the asker's preferences' blur together, and both the reinterpretations and the avoidance become intelligible as resistance to being clerked. So put the office on rotation — a week or a month at a time — making each of the three sometime designer and sometime subject. This changes the recommended conversation with the avoidant friend rather than replacing it: keep it one-on-one and non-accusing, but ask about stakes, not difficulty — do you want the flat at this standard at all, or is that our project being run on you? The answers diverge usefully: someone who wants a lower floor needs a trade, not a better-run talk.

Fourth move: where stakes genuinely differ, trade rather than enforce. If one person simply cares less about cleanliness, no record and no rota changes that, and enforcement aimed at low stakes produces withdrawal — which may be exactly what 'started avoiding the conversations' is. Price the difference instead: a lower common floor; or cleaning load swapped against the admin nobody wants — bills, shopping, landlord calls; or a small rent adjustment. The account on offer reaches for money only as a last resort; on the stakes framing, trade across domains is a first-class tool, not a defeat.

Honest costs, because the trade is real: whole-domain ownership is less flexible under shifting schedules than the account's weekly swap planning. Deputy defaults — if the owner is away, the area falls to a named person, never to nobody — and monthly rather than weekly adjustment are partial answers, not a full one. And the rotation doubles as a diagnostic: if the friend re-engages when it is their week in the chair, the withdrawal tracked the structure; if they withdraw even while holding the chair, the cause probably is not the chores at all, and the one-on-one conversation becomes the necessary move rather than a supplement.

What survives from the account on offer: the written record, relocated from the conversation to the site of the work; the periodic look, chaired in rotation; the one-on-one ask, question changed; the caution against over-engineering; the structural exits. What changes is where the load sits — in ownership, point-of-use specification and office — rather than in better-convened talk.",

Claims, criticisms and methods are fallible. Do not invent a source, an observation, an earlier event, or a dependency to fill a field. A missing view says what you can currently see; it does not establish what happened earlier. Return a JSON object with exactly two independently authored string fields: body and commitments. Body is your public prose contribution. Commitments says what taking your contribution up would involve. An empty commitment surface is allowed when none can be identified. Do not repeat the body wholesale into commitments.

Use FCL-1 for the commitment surface, encoded as a JSON document inside the commitments string: {"language":"FCL-1","records":[...],"uptake":[...]}. Each record has unique local id, type (claim|commitment|objection|use|problem), and text (unrestricted prose). Optional prose fields: scope, action, consequence, grounds, bearing. Optional arrays of references: target, depends, mentions, revises, withdraws. References are local IDs or exposed-artifact-label#local-ID; do not invent hidden IDs. A commitment proposes a scoped use, action, application or consequence; an objection alleges a defect whose bearing can itself be criticized; a use proposes an uptake or response; a problem states an unresolved question. depends asserts reliance; mentions only locates material. uptake lists the records you currently propose to use, not certified truths. No record type or optional field must be present. Empty records and uptake are allowed. Express uncertainty or an unrepresentable relation in prose rather than inventing a relation. The body remains unrestricted prose.

Return one JSON object with exactly two string fields: "body" and "commitments". Write the actual commitments separately; do not copy the body into that field as a storage shortcut.

# rival

Explore another way of posing or addressing the problem. You see the account's body; its commitment field is not supplied.

## Original problem (task)
[01274f41553299e7] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

BODY
The material contains four separable features, and it is worth keeping them separate because they call for different moves: recurring arguments over chores; agreements whose meaning gets contested later; work schedules that keep changing; and one friend now avoiding the conversations.

The most tractable is the contested-meaning problem. If you agree on who but not on what, when, or to what standard, later dispute is the expected outcome, not a mystery. 'You said you'd do the kitchen' can have meant wipe the counters tonight or deep-clean by Sunday, and both parties can honestly remember their version. A less charitable reading — someone reinterpreting to escape a load — is also possible, and the same remedy covers both cases without accusing anyone: capture the agreement in writing at the moment it is made. Task, concrete standard, deadline, somewhere all three can see. The asker can start this unilaterally: after any chore conversation, post a short confirmation — just so we're aligned, I've got X by Friday night, you've got Y by Sunday — that the others can correct on the spot. Once disputes are about a shared text rather than about memories, they get shorter even if nobody's motives improve.

Shifting schedules make fixed assignments brittle: a static rota either goes stale or lands unfairly. What fits that instability is short-horizon planning — a brief weekly look at who is actually around — plus an explicit swap rule: if your schedule changes, say so and propose a swap; do not let a task silently lapse. Silence after a schedule change is plausibly where a chunk of the later 'what did we agree' trouble originates.

The avoidance is the part where guessing is most tempting and most dangerous. One conjecture worth testing: if chore conversations only get convened when something has gone wrong, then 'let's talk about the chores' has become a synonym for complaint, and the friend may be avoiding being complained at — not the chores, not the asker. The word 'started' suggests this is a change rather than a fixed trait, which points toward something in the situation having shifted, possibly the character of the conversations themselves. If the conjecture holds, making the conversation routine, short, and mostly forward-looking (planning and swaps rather than audits) changes what it signals and may lower its cost. But that is a conjecture; the material does not say why the friend avoids the talks, and the difference matters — feeling ganged up on, feeling outvoted two-to-one, disengagement from the flat, and something entirely outside the chores each call for different responses. The move that fits the uncertainty is to ask, one-on-one and without accusation, what makes those conversations hard — and to do it before designing any system for that person rather than with them.

A caution against over-engineering: among friends, a visible enforcement apparatus can itself become the grievance, and the friendship is a bigger asset than any cleaning rota. Whatever system gets built should be minimal, jointly designed by all three so that it is ours rather than mine, and cheap to drop if it costs more goodwill than it saves.

One more conjecture worth testing quietly: chore arguments often run on a perception asymmetry — everyone sees their own contributions and few of anyone else's. If any of the arguing is about who does more, a shared visible record partially corrects each person's evidence. If the arguments are purely about task meaning, the record helps anyway.

And a fallback worth holding open rather than treating as defeat: if a fair, minimal, jointly adopted system is tried in good faith and the friction persists, the remaining options are structural — split a cleaner three ways, since money splits are more legible than labor splits; shrink the shared surface so there is less to argue about; or renegotiate whether the living arrangement is working. Those are legitimate endpoints, not failures.

In short: write agreements down as they are made; plan weekly against real schedules with a swap rule; ask the avoidant friend what is hard before assuming; keep the system light and jointly owned; and keep structural exits in view.

A JSON object carrying "body" and "commitments". Both are strings and nothing else is required.
